new_statements.rule_in_words: Kisetla keeps the Swahili penultimate word stress as its default; a subset of words (the example is mwafrika 'an African', stressed on the antepenult after English 'African') take English stress placement instead. Heine 1973's sketch of Kenya-Pidgin-Swahili (his cover term for kisetla + kihindi) says the same from the other side: the word prosodeme (stress + slight lengthening, often raised pitch) is bound to the penultimate syllable, no distinctive prosodemes, with antepenult or final placement in some Arabic and English loanwords.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any recovered snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: Muthiani: 'some words in Kisetla take the English stress' (mwafrika example, scanned-garbled). Heine 1973 fn. 73 (KPS): some words, mostly Arabic and English loans, carry the word prosodeme on the antepenult or final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Muthiani's subsection is 'Stress' under phonology; Heine's prosodeme is defined per 'Worteinheit' and is the basis of the phonological word in KPS). Heine adds phrase-level question and emphasis prosodemes on the same penultimate syllable, differing by tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All descriptions concern the pidgin Swahili used between European settlers and African workers in the Kenya highlands (Kisetla/Kisettla, 'Up-country' or 'Kitchen' Swahili), although Glottolog/Ethnologue place sett1235 [sta] in Zambia. Heine 1973's stress statement is for his 'Kenya-Pidgin-Swahili' (KPS), a cover term he defines as comprising kisetla (settler pidgin) and kihindi (Indian-shopkeeper pidgin, cf. cutc1238 Cutchi-Swahili), so it is not Kisetla-specific. Muthiani 1974 and Vitale 1980 describe Kisetla proper.
